name: Anywa
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Lusted, Marie. 1976. Anywa. In M. Lionel Bender (ed.), The Non-Semitic Languages of Ethiopia (Monograph No. 5, Occasional Papers Series, Committee on Ethiopian Studies), 495-512. East Lansing: African Studies Center, Michigan State University.
catalog_locator: §2.3 'Other Features': stress statement on p. 499; word-shape and tone statements on p. 498
catalog_quote: Stress in words of more than one syllable is on the stem syllable, or the one containing the consonant(s). a'wal 'rɛ̈ɛ̈o 'rɛmo a'bila 'ɔtɔ. If we take some examples from loan words, it would seem that stress can be on any syllable: 'gimmira 'tax' from Amharic gɨbɨr; dða'baɲɲa 'policeman' from Amharic zəbəɲɲa; alaatθ'kɛ̈ɛ̈r 'soldier' from Arabic ʔal askari. [p. 498, §2.3] Most words in Anywa are monosyllabic, an average of sixty percent, according to Keefer (1976:166). The CVC pattern is the most common, but there are also CV or VC monosyllabic words, and many cases where a or o is prefixed, and/or a, o, or ɛ suffixed. ... There are no consonant clusters. Tone is an important feature of Anywa, both gramatically and, less frequently, lexically. It has not been studied extensively, and is not indicated in the present orthography. A high and a low tone have been recognized (' and ` respectively).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Anywa is a tone language (high vs low per Lusted; two tonemes per Hieda 1994; four-way per Wikipedia summarising Reh 1996). Most words are monosyllabic (CVC). In polysyllabic native words stress falls on the stem (root) syllable, i.e. the syllable containing the root consonant(s), not on the vocalic prefixes/suffixes (a-, o-, -o, -ɛ etc.): a'wal 'gourd', a'bila 'hut', 'rɛmo 'blood', 'ɔtɔ 'house'. In loanwords (Amharic, Arabic) stress can be on any syllable, i.e. it follows the source language.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords: stress can be on any syllable ('gimmira 'tax' < Amharic gɨbɨr; dʒa'baŋŋa 'policeman' < Amharic zebeŋŋa; alaatθ'kɛ̈ɛ̈r 'soldier' < Arabic ʔal askari).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in a short phonology sketch (5 pp.); tone is treated separately as the important prosodic feature (high/low, grammatical > lexical). No instrumental evidence; Lusted was an SIL-affiliated field worker and the sketch pre-dates the full description (Reh 1996), which was not obtainable and may not recognise word stress at all.
new_statements.identity_note: Lusted 1976 describes Anywa of Ethiopia (Gambela area; she names the dialects Adongo, Ciro, Lul, Openo but does not tie the sketch to one of them) = anua1242. Hieda 1994 is based on Akobo-river (Sudan) speakers of the same language. No separate glottocode involved.

tone_statements.citation: Trommer, Jochen. 2016. Polarity, floating tones and the OCP in Anywa. Paper abstract, Thirteenth Old World Conference in Phonology (OCP13), Budapest, 13-16 January 2016. 2 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Data: H-tones in Anywa trigger basically two e↵ects at morpheme boundaries: Rightwards-spreading to a L-tone syllable (/ká:t-Ò/ ‘weave:sth:there-INF’ ! [kát-Ó])) and insertion of a L-tone before another H-tone resulting in a rising tone in a monosyllabic and a H-L sequence in a bisyllabic prosodic word (/Ú-máth-à/ ! [Ú-màth-á] HAB-drink:AP-1SG ‘whenever I drink’). Crucially, both processes also happen after lexical floating H-tones which appear at the end of many L-tone syllables (Reh 1993 calls L-tone syllables with a following floating H ‘mid tone’ syllables).
tone_statements.translation: (English; extracted text artefacts: 'e↵ects' = 'effects', '!' = the mapping arrow ->)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: 2 lexical tones H/L + lexical floating H (surface 'mid' = L with trailing floating H per Reh); rising contour derived by L-insertion before H (OCP/polarity), no falling tones; rightward H spreading root->suffix; grammatical/affixal floating tones; TBU = syllable.

tone_statements.citation: Trommer, Jochen. 2011. Phonological aspects of Western Nilotic mutation morphology. Habilitationsschrift, Universitaet Leipzig. (PDF '' on the author's Leipzig homepage.)
tone_statements.quote: Reh (1993:47) assumes that Anywa in addition to a L(ow) and a H(igh) tone also has a M(id) tone which is phonetically usually indistinguishable from a L tone, but behaves phonologically quite differently ... In the following, I will argue that M-tone morphemes are actually associated to a L tone followed by a floating H tone. ... Single morphemes in Anywa either carry L or H tone, but never a contour tone (see Reh 199345 on some potential exceptions). A rising tone may however result from sandhi processes
tone_statements.summary: OT reanalysis of Reh 1993's data: two tones L and H; Reh's 'mid' = L plus floating H; rising contours only from sandhi (word-final), no falling contours; no downstep; nothing on Anywa stress.

[kát-Ó])) and insertion of a L-tone before another H-tone resulting in a rising tone in a monosyllabic and a H-L sequence in a bisyllabic prosodic word (/Ú-máth-à/ ! sources.note: Full text (abstract) read: Anywa has H and L tones plus lexical floating H tones after many L syllables (Reh's 'mid tone' reanalysed as L + floating H); H spreads rightward from root to suffix (/ka:t-O/ -> [kat-O] with H), a (floating or linked) H before another H triggers OCP-driven L-insertion giving a rising tone on a monosyllable or H-L on a disyllable ('polarity'), falling tones are excluded; asymmetries between prefix-root, root-suffix and compound boundaries; OT analysis in Colored Containment with recursive prosodic words.
